title: Emotional Experience and Adherence in Chess Games Against Human and Avatar-AI Opponents in Patients with Affective Disorders
summary:
Background:
Playing chess can have a positive impact on mental fitness and well-being. For individuals with mental illnesses, particularly depressive disorders, chess could therefore offer a simple and enjoyable way to stay occupied and cognitively active during an inpatient hospital stay. New technologies and artificial intelligence make it possible to develop computer-controlled figures (avatars) that can speak and react like a real conversation partner. Whether the gaming experience against such a figure is perceived similarly to playing against a real human has, so far, been little researched.
Research Question:
This pilot study investigates how patients with depressive disorders experience playing chess, both against a real human opponent and against an avatar. Among other factors, the study examines how satisfied the participants are with the game, how they feel during play, and whether they voluntarily choose to play longer.
Methodology:
Forty patients with depressive disorders who are undergoing inpatient treatment will participate in the study. Each participant will play chess games against two different opponents: once against a real human opponent at a physical chessboard, and once against an avatar on a screen. The order in which the two conditions are played is randomized. After each game, participants fill out brief questionnaires describing their experiences and state of well-being.

criteria:
Inclusion criteria:
Ability to provide written informed consent and willingness to participate in the study
Sufficient proficiency in German to understand instructions, complete questionnaires, and engage in interactions
Basic computer literacy (mouse/keyboard operation)
Diagnosis of an affective disorder as documented by the treating physician
Exclusion criteria:
Clinical condition that prevents safe participation
Severe cognitive impairment (e.g., dementia, delirium) or neurological disorders that significantly impair task performance
Lack of sufficient proficiency in German
